Introduction

Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) integrates mindfulness practices with cognitive strategies to alleviate perceived stress and its associated symptoms. While well studied in adults, evidence for schoolbased MBCT among adolescents with psychosomatic complaints—particularly in China—remains limited.

Methods

We conducted a quasi-experimental, mixed-methods study in three public secondary schools in DaZhou (Sichuan, China). Female students aged 14–16 were screened (N = 1,200) using the Psychosomatic Complaints Scale (PCS; cutoff > 45) and DSM-5–informed clinical interviews; 60 eligible students were randomly allocated to MBCT or school-as-usual control. The primary outcomes were the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS; α = 0.85) and the PCS (α = 0.86). Parent (n = 6) and teacher (n = 5) interviews were analyzed thematically.

Results

Compared with controls, the MBCT group showed greater reductions in perceived stress and psychosomatic symptoms at post-test and two-month follow-up (Group×Time, p < .001; partial η²≈0.32–0.63). Mean reductions exceeded a conventional 0.5 SD benchmark.

Conclusion

School-delivered MBCT was associated with sustained improvements in perceived stress and psychosomatic complaints among 14–16-year-old girls, with convergent qualitative evidence from parents and teachers. Interpretation remains cautious given the passive control, short follow-up, and bounded generalizability.

This study evaluates a school-based MBCT program for Chinese adolescents aged 14–16 with psychosomatic symptoms, testing its effectiveness in reducing perceived stress and improving mental health. Outcomes are triangulated using adolescent self-reports and streamlined evaluations from parents and teachers to establish ecological validity within everyday school and home environments.

H1 MBCT produces a significant Group (MBCT vs. control) × Time (baseline, post-test, follow-up) interaction on the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) and the Psychosomatic Complaints Scale (PCS), with greater reductions in the MBCT group.
H2 After adjustment for baseline (and prespecified covariates), the MBCT group shows lower PSS and PCS means than the control group at post-test and follow-up.
H3 A higher proportion of MBCT participants achieves clinically meaningful improvement on PSS and PCS (e.g., ≥ 0.5 SD reduction or reliable change) than controls.
H4 = parents and teachers report improvements in students’ emotion regulation, coping, classroom functioning, and management of somatic complaints after MBCT relative to control.

An a priori power analysis (G*Power 3.1) indicated that 26 participants per group provide 0.80 power to detect a medium effect (f = 0.25) at α = 0.05; thus, the randomized sample is adequate. Three participants withdrew (two experimental, one control), leaving 57 completers (28 experimental, 29 control). Eligibility required: PCS > 45; no current psychiatric medication/psychotherapy; age 14–16 years; student assent and guardian consent; and commitment to session attendance. Exclusion criteria were > 3 absences, disqualifying medical conditions, or refusal to complete follow-up. Group means did not differ at baseline on key measures.

The Psychosomatic Complaints Scale (PCS) consists of 30 items, each scored on a 4-point Likert scale, with total scores ranging from 0 to 90. A cutoff score of 45 indicates potential psychosomatic dysfunction. Initial studies reported a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.64 and confirmed a unifactorial structure with one factor explaining 34.1% of the variance. Hajloo [63] confirmed its one-dimensionality (KMO = 0.782) and high reliability (α = 0.85; r = .85 for test–retest reliability). In the present study, the PCS underwent further psychometric evaluation, yielding a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.86 and acceptable model fit indices in confirmatory factor analysis (CFI = 0.93, RMSEA = 0.06), thus empirically supporting its reliability and validity for the Chinese adolescent sample.

The Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) consists of 14 items, each rated on a 5-point scale (0 = “never” to 4 = “very often”), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 56. Internal consistency in the original development sample ranged from 0.84 to 0.86 [65]. Broton et al. [42] achieved acceptable reliability (α = 0.81 in the Iranian sample and 0.86 in the American sample). The Cronbach’s alpha in this study was 0.85, confirming satisfactory internal consistency. A confirmatory factor analysis further validated the two-factor structure of the PSS (CFI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.05).

Attrition was low (three withdrawals), and an attrition analysis showed no baseline differences between completers and non-completers. For quantitative outcomes, we used mixed ANOVA (Group × Time) with assumption checks and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons, reporting partial η² and confidence intervals. Missingness was low (< 5%) and passed Little’s MCAR test; nevertheless, given known biases of LOCF, we used multiple imputation as our primary strategy: m = 20 datasets via fully conditional specification (predictive mean matching for continuous variables), including Group, Time, outcomes at all waves, and covariates in the imputation model. Estimates were pooled using Rubin’s rules. We performed LOCF and complete-case analyses as sensitivity checks; the conclusions remained unchanged across both approaches.

Table 2 Means and standard deviations of perceived stress and mental health across the three time points in experimental and control groups
| Variable       | Group        | Pre-test (M ± SD) | Post-test (M ± SD) | Follow-up (M ± SD) |
|:---------------|:-------------|:------------------|:-------------------|:-------------------|
| Perceived Stress | Experimental | 35.33 ± 6.12      | 28.55 ± 6.58       | 29.50 ± 6.46       |
|                | Control      | 33.42 ± 4.79      | 34.36 ± 4.49       | 34.05 ± 4.58       |
| Mental Health  | Experimental | 55.83 ± 7.94      | 49.66 ± 7.53       | 49.94 ± 7.58       |
|                | Control      | 57.21 ± 6.55      | 57.84 ± 6.67       | 57.94 ± 6.85       |

For perceived stress, students in the experimental group reported a significant reduction from pre-test (M = 35.33, SD = 6.12, 95% CI [33.01, 37.65]) to post-test (M = 28.55, SD = 6.58, 95% CI [26.06, 31.04]). Although scores slightly increased at follow-up (M = 29.50, SD = 6.46, 95% CI [27.06, 31.94]), they remained well below baseline levels. By contrast, the control group showed no meaningful change across time points (pre-test: M = 33.42, SD = 4.79, 95% CI [31.77, 35.07]; post-test: M = 34.36, SD = 4.49, 95% CI [32.82, 35.90]; follow-up: M = 34.05, SD = 4.58, 95% CI [32.49, 35.61]). Using a distribution-based benchmark of ≥ 0.5 SD for clinical importance (≈ 3.06 on PSS), the experimental group’s mean reductions from pre-test to post-test (Δ = 6.78) and to follow-up (Δ = 5.83) exceeded this threshold, suggesting potential clinical relevance beyond statistical significance.

A similar pattern emerged for mental health (where lower scores reflect fewer symptoms). The experimental group improved from pre-test (M = 55.83, SD = 7.94, 95% CI [52.71, 58.95]) to post-test (M = 49.66, SD = 7.53, 95% CI [46.70, 52.62]) and maintained this gain at follow-up (M = 49.94, SD = 7.58, 95% CI [46.97, 52.91]). In contrast, the control group’s mental health scores remained virtually unchanged (pre-test: M = 57.21, SD = 6.55, 95% CI [54.93, 59.49]; post-test: M = 57.84, SD = 6.67, 95% CI [55.53, 60.15]; follow-up: M = 57.94, SD = 6.85, 95% CI [55.58, 60.30]). Applying the same ≥ 0.5 SD benchmark (≈ 3.97 on this scale), the experimental group’s mean reductions (pre→post Δ = 6.17; pre→follow-up Δ = 5.89) met or exceeded the criterion, supporting applied interpretability of the changes.

To test for statistical significance, a mixed-design ANOVA (2 × 3) was conducted (Table 3). For perceived stress, there was a significant main effect of time, F(2, 112) = 35.75, p < .0001, partial η² = 0.50, 95% CI [0.36, 0.60]; a significant main effect of group, F(1, 56) = 28.42, p < .0001, partial η² = 0.48, 95% CI [0.31, 0.58]; and a highly significant time × group interaction, F(2, 112) = 59.96, p < .0001, partial η² = 0.63, 95% CI [0.51, 0.70]. For mental health, significant effects were also found for time, F(2, 112) = 20.38, p < .0001, partial η² = 0.37, 95% CI [0.22, 0.49]; for group, F(1, 56) = 16.47, p < .0001, partial η² = 0.32, 95% CI [0.16, 0.45]; and for the time × group interaction, F(2, 112) = 32.05, p < .0001, partial η² = 0.48, 95% CI [0.33, 0.58]. Adjusted mixed-effects models that controlled for baseline PSS/PCS, age, and school replicated all inferences, and multiple-imputation–pooled estimates converged with complete-case and LOCF sensitivity analyses (see Appendix), strengthening robustness.

Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons (Table 4) confirmed that perceived stress significantly decreased between pre-test and post-test (Mean Difference = 2.91, p = .001, 95% CI [1.88, 3.94]) and between pre-test and follow-up (Mean Difference = 2.60, p = .001, 95% CI [1.55, 3.65]); the small increase between post-test and follow-up (Mean Difference = − 0.31, p = .21) was not significant, indicating sustained stress reduction. For mental health, significant improvements were found from pre-test to post-test (Mean Difference = 2.76, p = .001, 95% CI [1.72, 3.80]) and from pre-test to follow-up (Mean Difference = 2.57, p = .001, 95% CI [1.48, 3.66]), with no significant change between post-test and follow-up (Mean Difference = − 0.19, p = .75). Within-group Bonferroni tests indicated that time contrasts were significant for the experimental group but not for the control group, adding precision to the interpretation that change was intervention-linked rather than due to measurement fluctuation.

These findings collectively confirm that MBCT led to significant and sustained improvements in both perceived stress and mental health among students with psychosomatic symptoms. The lack of substantial differences between post-test and follow-up scores supports the durability of the intervention’s effects over two months. Average reductions exceeded a half–standard deviation on both outcomes, a commonly used distribution-based marker of clinically meaningful change. No participant attrition occurred between post-test and follow-up, ensuring consistency in sample size and enhancing the reliability of longitudinal comparisons.

Thematic analysis of interviews with 11 informants (6 parents and 5 teachers) yielded six overarching themes. Teacher 4 noted that “two students still avoid class participation under stress,” suggesting that MBCT may require adaptation for those with more entrenched anxiety patterns or social withdrawal tendencies. Parent 2 noted, “Although my child is more selfaware, I wouldn’t say they’re emotionally resilient yet—it’s a work in progress.” Teacher 5 pointed out, “Some students remain socially reserved despite the intervention,” indicating that while MBCT may enhance social-emotional awareness, individual personality factors, such as introversion or past social experiences, may moderate its impact. Parent 6 remarked, “The academic improvements are there, but they’re slower compared to changes in mood or behavior.” Teacher 2 noted challenges in habit formation: “Some students say they forget to use the techniques when stressed, which shows that reinforcement might still be needed.” Parent 6 admitted, “He used to meditate daily, but now only does it when reminded.”

The findings suggest that MBCT had a significant positive impact on reducing perceived stress and improving mental health, aligning with previous studies supporting mindfulness interventions for psychological distress [1, 2]. In applied terms, the observed mean reductions exceeded a conventional half-standard-deviation benchmark in this sample, which strengthens the case for clinical relevance; however, this threshold is heuristic and should be interpreted cautiously alongside confidence intervals. However, the small sample size, quasi-experimental design, and lack of an active control group limit the generalizability of these findings. These factors, alongside the absence of blinding, may have contributed to potential placebo effects; therefore, future studies should incorporate larger, randomized controlled trials to isolate the specific effects of MBCT more effectively. Specifically, expectancy and attention effects could inflate between-group contrasts when controls receive less contact; detection bias is also plausible when assessors are not fully blinded. These risks may bias estimates upward, implying that our effects represent an upper bound under these design constraints.

The primary outcome of reduced perceived stress found in this study corroborates findings by Porcelli et al. [3]. The findings of this study are also consistent with recent evidence supporting the effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions in reducing psychological distress and improving emotion regulation. For example, Feng et al. [67] demonstrated that mindfulness significantly reduced parenting stress among parents of children with autism, with resilience and psychological flexibility mediating this effect. Similarly, Zhang et al. [68] showed that mindfulness helped Chinese university students manage academic stress and improve emotional intelligence. A meta-analysis by Ng et al. [69] confirmed that mindfulness-based interventions are highly effective in reducing psychological symptoms in high school adolescents. Additionally, Lan et al. [70] found that mindfulness combined with life-skills training helped improve emotion regulation and reduce anxiety symptoms among Chinese migrant children.

The second significant finding concerns the improvement in mental health outcomes for students with psychosomatic disorders. This aligns with findings from Lan et al. [9], Petrenko et al. [2], and Martin et al. [11]. While these findings are significant, the absence of a placebo or active control group, as well as the lack of blinding in this study, are substantial limitations that could affect the robustness of the conclusions. Moreover, the relative stability of the control group could reflect valid invariance, regression to the mean, or minor expectancy effects from administrative contact; an attention-matched or education-based comparator would help disentangle specific from non-specific benefits.

In conclusion, this study contributes valuable insights into the potential of MBCT to reduce stress and improve mental health among adolescents with psychosomatic symptoms. By integrating both quantitative outcomes and qualitative insights from parents and teachers, the research offers a comprehensive view of the impact of MBCT on adolescents’ well-being. However, the study’s limitations, such as the small sample size, the quasi-experimental design, and the lack of an active control group, suggest that these findings should be interpreted with caution. Generalizability is bounded by setting (three public schools in DaZhou), age (14–16), and gender (female), and the design likely overestimates effects relative to fully blinded, attention-matched RCTs. To strengthen the validity of future research, studies should utilize randomized controlled trials, include larger and more diverse samples, and incorporate extended follow-up periods to assess the durability of the intervention’s effects. Specifically, we advocate for multi-arm trials comparing MBCT with an attention-matched health education control, preregistered mediator analyses (decentering, rumination, resilience), and moderator analyses (baseline avoidance, practice dose, instructor fidelity), as well as cost-effectiveness assessments, to inform school policy.

summarised_markdown:
Objectives: We examined stress, burnout, and sleeping troubles among mental health professionals in the context of psychosocial risk factors related to participation in COVID care during the fourth and ﬁfth waves.

Materials and methods: Mental health professionals (N=268) completed an online cross-sectional survey in Hungary, between November 2021 and April 2022. Of the respondents, 58.2% directly participated in COVID care. The main data collection instrument was the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ II), including 20 subscales on work-related psychosocial factors and 3 outcome scales (stress, burnout, and sleeping troubles).

Results: Participation in COVID care was associated with higher work pace (59.08 versus 49.78), more role conﬂicts (55.21 versus 45.93), lower scores on the inﬂuence at work (38.18 versus 51.79), predictability (44.71 versus 57.03), reward (55.82 versus 65.03), role clarity (70.19 versus 75.37), social support from supervisor (59.24 versus 65.55), job satisfaction (54.36 versus 62.84), trust regarding management (55.89 versus 67.86), justice and respect (44.51 versus 54.35) scales. Among those involved in COVID care, only the stress score was higher (47.96 vs. 42.35) in the total sample; however, among psychiatrists, both stress (52.16 vs. 38.60) and burnout scores (58.30 vs. 47.06) were higher.

Stepwise multiple regression revealed that work-family conﬂict, emotional demands and workplace commitment were independent predictors of higher stress and burnout scores; furthermore, competence transgression had a signiﬁcant effect on stress, and being a psychiatric specialist had a signiﬁcant effect on burnout. These models explained 40.5% of the variance for stress and 39.8% for burnout.

Conclusion: During the fourth and ﬁfth waves, although COVID care was more well-organized, psychiatrists, as specialist physicians responsible for the quality of the care, were still experiencing challenges regarding their competence and inﬂuence at work, which may explain their increased levels of stress and burnout.

The aim of our study was to evaluate work-related psychosocial risk factors in COVID care units in comparison to non-COVID care units among mental health professionals in Hungary. Measured mental health indicators were stress, burnout, and sleeping troubles; we aimed to analyze their associations with work-related psychosocial factors in the context of participation in COVID care.

Methods

We conducted a cross-sectional survey between November 15, 2021 and April 15, 2022. Our target group was mental health professionals working in psychiatric and psychotherapeutic care in Hungary. We estimate that approximately 10% of health care professionals working at psychiatry care units in Hungary responded to the survey.

As our main data collection instrument, we employed the Hungarian version of the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ II). We included 20 subscales on psychosocial work environment, 3 or 4 items each, and 3 outcome scales: stress, burnout, and sleeping troubles. In our sample, the internal consistency of the subscales was good or acceptable, ranging from 0.656 to 0.916.

Additionally, we included an item on competence transgression: “In your opinion, to what extent are your overall professional competencies violated during your work?” The response options were: “to a great extent/to a moderate extent/to a small extent/not at all”.

Items on sociodemographic and professional background included sex, age, occupation, specialization, years of work experience in specialty, location of workplace (capital or countryside), and whether work was performed in COVID care.

Analyses were conducted using the IBM SPSS 26.0 software package. We used the Pearson correlation coefficient to determine the correlations between work-related psychosocial factors and stress and burnout. As a multivariate analysis, we conducted a linear regression analysis with the stepwise method to evaluate the independent effects of the relevant psychosocial factors.

Our survey was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Semmelweis University (SE-TUKEB: 270-1/2017).

Results

A total of 268 Hungarian persons, 208 women (77.6%) and 60 men (22.4%) completed the online questionnaire. The characteristics of the sample are presented in Table 2. Regarding occupation, there were 86 physicians (32% of the sample), 37 (13.8%) residents, 47 psychologists (17.5%), 84 nurses (31.3%), and 14 persons with a degree classified as “other”.

Overall, 156 respondents (58.21%) participated in COVID care. There were significant group differences concerning occupation: 78% of psychiatry residents, 67% of nurses, and 60% of psychiatrists worked in COVID care, while this proportion was only around 30% for psychologists and “other” professionals. We found no significant regional difference in their involvement in COVID care.

The comparison of mental health professionals involved in and those not involved in COVID care revealed several differences regarding work-related psychosocial factors (see Table 1). We found significantly higher mean scores for work pace (59.08 versus 49.78) and role conflicts (55.21 versus 45.93) among those working in COVID care. Those who participated in COVID care had significantly lower scores for influence at work (38.18 versus 51.79), predictability (44.71 versus 57.03), reward (55.82 versus 65.03), role clarity (70.19 versus 75.37), social support from supervisor (59.24 versus 65.55), job satisfaction (54.36 versus 62.84), trust regarding management (55.89 versus 67.86), as well as justice and respect (44.51 versus 54.35). Regarding mental health indicators, only the stress score was significantly higher among COVID care workers (47.96 ± 21.73 compared to 42.35 ± 22.14), while there were no significant differences in burnout and sleeping troubles scores.

Only psychiatry specialists exhibited significant differences in stress and burnout scores. Those involved in COVID care had a higher mean stress score (52.16 ± 22.41 versus 38.60 ± 19.55; p=0.005) and a higher mean burnout score (58.30 ± 23.54 vs. 47.06 ± 23.40; p=0.033) compared to those not involved in COVID care.

We also compared the professional groups to each other (Table 3) and found a significant difference (p=0.001) only in sleeping troubles: nurses scored higher (M=41.67, SD=25.73) compared to the other professional groups (psychiatrists: M=31.90, SD=24.48; psychiatry residents: M=26.18, SD=16.66; psychologists: M=25.27, SD=22.04). We found no difference in terms of burnout or stress.

A correlation analysis (Table 4) was conducted. The strongest correlations were found with emotional demands and work-family conflict (emotional demands with stress: r=0.380, with burnout: r=0.376; while work-family conflict with stress: r=0.543, with burnout: r=0.540). Among psychosocial factors, workplace commitment negatively correlated with stress (r=-0.313, p<0.001) and burnout (r=-0.283, p<0.001). Influence at work exhibited a significant correlation with stress (r=-0.2, p=0.001) and burnout (r=-0.212, p<0.001).

Lastly, employing multivariate analysis, we tested the predictors of stress and burnout (Table 5). This model explained 40.5% of the variance for stress and 39.8% for burnout (adjusted R squares: stress 39.6%, burnout 38.9%).

Stress levels were significantly influenced linearly by workfamily conflict, emotional demands, competence transgression, and workplace commitment. The degree of burnout was significantly affected by work-family conflict, emotional demands, workplace commitment, and by being a psychiatry specialist.

Discussion

We compared work-related psychosocial factors among mental health professionals involved in and those not involved in COVID care. Those involved in COVID care scored their work environment as necessitating a higher work pace and instigating more role conflicts, being less predictable, having less influence on their actual work, less justice and respect, yielding less rewards, and also having less trust regarding management and being less satisfied with the leadership (Table 1). We found that in the case of psychiatric workers participating in COVID care, they were associated only with slightly elevated stress levels; however, no significant difference was found in terms of burnout. Thus, our study indicates that participation in COVID care does not in itself cause burnout.

Our results showed no significant difference in stress and burnout between nurses and other mental health professionals. In our study, stress and burnout scores for each professional group (see Table 3) exhibited similar values. Of our sample of psychiatric workers, 58.2% was directly involved in COVID care. According to another Hungarian study (7), unpredictability was higher among nonphysician health care workers compared to physicians, but no significant difference was found between physicians and nonphysicians in terms of stress and burnout. Lasalvia et al. (51, 52) state that the burnout of psychiatrists in mental health teams is the highest, however, our study did not confirm this claim. A study from Saudi Arabia (53) investigated burnout among psychiatry residents during the pandemic, which described a lower prevalence (27.3%) compared to a pre-pandemic systematic review (33.7%) (54).

Regarding sleep quality, in our study, nurses scored significantly higher on the sleeping troubles subscale than psychiatrists, psychiatry residents, and psychologists. According to Cabeza et al.’s study in Columbia, during the first waves of the COVID-19 pandemic, psychiatrists and psychologists had more sleeping troubles than nurses, albeit this difference was not significant (58). In the review and meta-analysis of Salari et al. (59), the prevalence of sleep disorders during COVID-19 was higher among physicians as well. An African study (60) asserted that 23.9% of psychiatric workers were affected by sleep problems but found no significant association with professional position.

Our study also showed that participation in COVID care alone did not cause stress or burnout. A new study asserts it is unlikely that COVID-19 has caused as much damage to the mental health of most people as previous research has suggested. This systematic review examined the ‘general mental health’ factor before and during COVID in the general population; no changes in terms of mental health were found based on 94,411 unique titles and abstracts including 137 unique studies from 134 cohorts (62).

In our study, competence transgression had a moderating role only for stress, but not for burnout. Workplace commitment was also found to have a moderating and negative effect on both stress and burnout. Emotional demands and work-family conflict had a moderating role in both stress and burnout. In our study, influence at work was selected out as a nonsignificant variable using the stepwise method. Ogütlü et al. (75) conducted research among Turkish psychiatrists, most of whom reported moderate or high levels of stress related to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the majority of them also experienced moderate or high levels of workand patient-related burnout, as well as lower levels of personal burnout.

Our results are in accordance with other findings stating that work-family conflict is related to burnout and stress. Kameg et al. surveyed mental health nurses (76), 64% of whom reported that the demands of their job often disrupted their family life; overall burnout scores remained moderate. We compared the psychosocial risk profile of 286 mental health professionals involved in and those not involved in COVID care at psychiatry units in various regions of Hungary.

Limitations

Our cross-sectional study supplied a snapshot of the psychosocial factors of mental health professionals, however, this research design provided no opportunity to explore longitudinal, causal relationships. Our questionnaire was aimed at a wide range of professionals working within psychiatric-psychotherapeutic care in Hungary, yet, because the number of respondents was relatively low, especially in some rural regions our survey cannot be considered representative. On the other hand, we think that our results can be generalized, as our sample included a similar number of respondents from various centers from the capital and from smaller settlements, and we found no regional differences in the main outcome variables. The online survey was active over a 5 month period, as data collection went less efﬁciently as we hoped. We can draw limited conclusions regarding the speciﬁc stress of the psychologists, as some of them provided teleconsultations and others were directly involved in COVID care “at the bedside”, or both. Another limitation of the study is that we evaluated stress and burnout based on COPSOQ II questionnaire subscales, which did not allow us to examine the individual components of burnout.

Conclusion

One important message of the study is that participation in COVID care was not a risk factor for stress and burnout per se, but that certain workplace factors played a pronounced role (e.g., workfamily conﬂict, emotional demands). Not only risk factors, but also protective factors, such as workplace commitment, merit further investigation. Rethinking competences and setting up competence lists could also be a protective factor against stress.

It is important for psychiatrists to assess burnout and intervene. The working conditions of psychiatric nurses need to be rethought, with a particular focus on their mental health. Further research on stress and burnout among psychiatric workers is needed.

We hope our research will provide a good foundation for further international comparative studies focusing on health care workers and mental health professionals.
